text: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the backbone of the web. It structures content and defines how it should be displayed in browsers. In this post, we’ll cover the essentials of HTML, including its syntax, common tags, and best practices for writing clean and semantic code.

title: Getting Started with HTML
text:
What is HTML?
HTML is a markup language, not a programming language. It uses tags to define elements on a webpage, such as headings, paragraphs, links, images, and more. Each tag has a specific purpose and can be nested within other tags to create complex structures.

title: Bivariate and Multivariate Analysis
text:
Multivariate Analysis
Multivariate analysis involves examining the relationships among three or more variables.
Here are some common techniques for both types of analysis:
We will use titanic, tips, iris, and flights datasets for our examples.

import seaborn as sns
import pandas as pd

titanic = sns.load_dataset('titanic')
tips = sns.load_dataset('tips')
flights = sns.load_dataset('flights')
iris = sns.load_dataset('iris')

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
Most developers I know are extraordinarily good at thinking in systems—at decomposing problems,
spotting edge cases, and reasoning about trade-offs. Yet the same people often tell me they
“can’t write.” I think they’ve confused polish with clarity, and that’s a fixable mistake.

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
Writing Is Thinking Made Visible
When you write, you’re not transcribing thoughts that are already finished. You’re discovering
what you actually think. The discipline of forming a sentence forces you to choose between
ideas, discard the weak ones, and commit to the strong ones.



A developer writing at a desk



“I write to find out what I think.”
— Joan Didion

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
Five Reasons Developers Should Blog

Teaching solidifies understanding. The “Feynman technique”—explain a concept simply until
you can’t—exposes every gap in your knowledge faster than any test.
Your future self will thank you. A post explaining how you solved a tricky CORS issue is a
personal reference you’ll return to, and it’ll save someone else three hours of debugging.
Writing compounds. Thirty posts means thirty permanent search-indexed artifacts of your
expertise. That’s a form of leverage most developers ignore entirely.
It builds professional credibility. Recruiters, hiring managers, and peers read blogs.
A thoughtful post demonstrates judgment in a way a résumé cannot.
It builds the habit of finishing things. A blog post has a clear done state. That’s
rarer and more valuable than it sounds.

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
section: Common Objections (and Why They Don’t Hold)
text:
Common Objections (and Why They Don’t Hold)
“I don’t have anything original to say.” You don’t need to be first. You need to be useful.
A beginner’s explanation of a hard topic is often more helpful than the expert’s, because you
remember what confused you.
“No one will read it.” Write for one person: your past self, six months ago. If it would
have helped you then, publish it.
“I don’t have time.” A 400-word post once a month is better than nothing. Write rough. Edit
once. Ship.

title: Why Every Developer Should Write
text:
How to Start
The tooling friction is lower than ever:

Quarto — code-friendly, renders to HTML, PDF, or slides from one source
Ghost — beautifully minimal hosted blogging
Obsidian Publish — if you already live in Obsidian

Pick whichever puts the least distance between you and the publish button. The best tool is the
one you’ll actually use.

“Amateurs sit and wait for inspiration. The rest of us just show up and get to work.”
— Stephen King, On Writing

title: Introduction to EDA
text: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is a crucial step in the data analysis process. It involves summarizing the main characteristics of a dataset, often using visual methods. The goal of EDA is to gain insights into the data, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and test hypotheses.

title: Introduction to EDA
text: Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) is a crucial step in the data analysis process. It involves summarizing the main characteristics of a dataset, often using visual methods. The goal of EDA is to gain insights into the data, identify patterns, detect anomalies, and test hypotheses.

title: Introduction to EDA
text:
Types of EDA

Univariate Analysis: This type of analysis focuses on a single variable. It includes techniques such as frequency distribution, measures of central tendency (mean, median, mode), and measures of dispersion (range, variance, standard deviation).
Bivariate Analysis: This analysis examines the relationship between two variables. Common techniques include scatter plots, correlation coefficients, and cross-tabulations.
Multivariate Analysis: This type of analysis involves more than two variables. Techniques include multiple regression, principal component analysis (PCA), and cluster analysis.

Distribution Plot
We can also use distribution plots to visualize the distribution of numerical data.


sns.displot(data=df, x="age", kde = True)









Box Plot
We use box plots to visualize the distribution of numerical data and identify outliers.


sns.boxplot(data=df, x="age")

title: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis
text:
Data analysis is one of the most in-demand skills of the decade, and Python’s ecosystem makes it
remarkably accessible. In this post we’ll cover the essentials: loading data with pandas,
exploring it visually with matplotlib, and running everything interactively in Jupyter.
crumbs: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis

title: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis
text:
Setting Up Your Environment
Before writing a single line of analysis code, you need a working environment. The fastest path
is a virtual environment with the three core packages installed.
python -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate      # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate
pip install pandas matplotlib jupyter






TipPro Tip



Always check for missing values with df.isnull().sum() before any analysis. Silently missing
data is the leading cause of misleading results.


Once installed, launch Jupyter with jupyter notebook and create a new Python 3 kernel.
crumbs: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis

title: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis
text:
Loading and Exploring Data
The first thing you’ll do in almost every project is load a CSV file and peek at its shape.
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

df = pd.read_csv("data.csv")
print(df.head())
After df.head() you’ll want a quick statistical summary:



Method
What it shows




df.shape
(rows, columns)


df.dtypes
data type per column


df.describe()
count, mean, std, min/max


df.isnull().sum()
missing values per column



These four lines form a reliable first-pass audit of any new dataset.
crumbs: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis

title: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis
text:
Visualising with Matplotlib
A histogram is the fastest way to understand the distribution of a numeric column.
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.hist(df["value_column"], bins=30, color="#3B82F6", edgecolor="white")
ax.set_title("Distribution of value_column")
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("distribution.png", dpi=150)
plt.show()

“A picture is worth a thousand words—and in data analysis, a good chart is worth a thousand
rows of summary statistics.”
— Hadley Wickham, R for Data Science
crumbs: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis

title: Getting Started with Python Data Analysis
text:
Next Steps
You now have the foundation. From here, the natural progressions are:

Seaborn for statistical plots with less boilerplate
Plotly for interactive, web-ready visualisations
scikit-learn when you’re ready to move from exploration to modelling
Polars as a faster alternative to pandas for large datasets

Keep iterating, keep plotting, and don’t be afraid to look at your data from five different
angles before drawing any conclusions.

What is CSS?
CSS is a stylesheet language that describes how HTML elements should be rendered on screen, in print, or other media. It separates the presentation of a document from its structure, making it easier to maintain and update the look and feel of a website.
